newsitem.title: JAPAN: Dlr falls vs yen by late Tokyo on trade fears.
newsitem.headline: Dlr falls vs yen by late Tokyo on trade fears.

text.p: 0620 GMT TRADED HIGH/LOW AS OF 0600 GMT

The dollar fell against the yen by late Tokyo on Wednesday on persistent sales after comments by the U.S. deputy treasury secretary raised concerns over Japan's trade surplus ahead of the G7 summit later this month.
Despite remarks by Japanese officials expressing concern over excessive currency movements, sentiment towards the dollar remained weak, dealers said.
The greenback fell as low as 110.81 yen, its lowest level since November 18, 1996. It ended at 112.17/22 yen in New York.

"Concern over a rise in Japan's trade surplus lingers, especially in the United States as it was seen in comments from (U.S. Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence) Summers today. Unless Japan deals with it appropriately, such concerns will keep weighing on the dollar," a trust bank dealer said.

Summers urged Japan to foster a domestic demand-led economic recovery at home, to avoid running up external surpluses that would hurt global growth, and to keep up efforts to deregulate and open its markets to foreign goods.
His remarks came after the Ministry of Finance (MOF) announced that Japan's current account surplus rose 92.7 percent to 1.09 trillion yen in April from a year earlier.

Although the figures were mostly within market expectations, prompting some dollar purchases in early trade, the market remained worried that Japan's trade surplus may continue to expand in May and after, keeping the dollar's topside heavy, dealers said.
Dealers expect the issue of Japan's current account surplus to be discussed at the Group of Seven industrialised nations' summit meeting in Denver on June 20-22.
U.S. funds, Japanese investors and interbank dealers were said to be the main sellers of the dollar, while no substantial bids were detected on the downside.
Japanese monetary authorities voiced concern about the dollar's volatile movement, but failed to stop the dollar's downward trend, dealers said.

A senior MOF official, Eisuke Sakakibara, was quoted by Jiji news agency as saying an excessively weak or strong yen is undesirable. His remarks were later echoed by Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka, who added that MOF would deal with foreign exchange movements in an appropriate manner, Jiji reported.

Dealers said Sakakibara's comments did not carry enough weight to push the dollar back above 112 yen and traders started selling again. "Now, it would not be a surprise if the dollar were to fall below 110 yen," the trust bank dealer said.
The yen remained well-bid against major currencies in crosses as well. The mark fell below 65 yen and was weak at 64.63/66 yen at 0704 GMT, compared with 65.35 yen in early Tokyo trading.
A dealer at a German bank said the mark was at a turning point against the yen, and a further fall in the dollar against the yen may send the mark/yen to a new range of 60-65 yen.

A European bank dealer in Singapore said: "There was a lot of dollar/yen selling by U.S. investment houses when the dollar broke 111.70 yen." He added that stop-loss sales were triggered around the 111.50 level.
The dollar also fell against the mark, but the dealer in Singapore said the greenback should find some support around 1.7080 marks.
The dollar closed at 1.7183/88 marks in New York on Tuesday.
